newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar rise to 44-month high in Tokyo hurts stocks.
newsitem.headline: Dollar rise to 44-month high in Tokyo hurts stocks.

text.p: The dollar rose above 115 yen in Tokyo on Thursday morning, its highest level in over 44 months, pushing already weak Tokyo stock prices lower.
It reached as high as 115.06 yen before settling at about 115.00 in late morning trade.

The dollar's rise sent the Tokyo stock market's benchmark Nikkei average of 225 leading shares reeling by 2.3 percent at midday, as already weak stocks were hurt further by the yen's fall and the spectre of selling by foreign investors, brokers said.
Dealers said triggering of dollar purchases just above 115 yen, placed in advance to cut losses on existing positions, was the direct cause of the dollar's rise.
But they said the greenback had been supported from morning trade on expectations of commercial purchases and fragile Tokyo share prices.

"There had been a substantial amount of Japanese importer purchases at the local fixing (at 0100 GMT) and then we had the fall of stock prices on top of that," said Hank Note, chief dealer with Sumitomo Bank.
Recent weakness in stock prices has strengthened the view that Japan will be forced to keep its interest rates at record lows, hurting yen sentiment and giving the dollar support.
The Nikkei average ended morning trade down 451.09 points at 19,098.32. It was the first time the Nikkei had fallen below the 19,000 level since December 6 last year.
The Nikkei initially dipped due to selling linked with the futures trading, brokers said.
"Since we don't know what will happen during the long holiday, some traders closed their positions in the morning," one broker said. The market will be closed from Tuesday until January 5.

Although Tokyo stocks rebounded on Wednesday, they have been battered since last week by worries about the effects on the economy of the government's tightening of fiscal policy to tackle Japan's budget deficit.
The government has decided to end special income tax cuts from January and raise the consumption tax next April, sparking fears in the market that a fledgling recovery in the economy may be damaged.
